description: We are a multidisciplinary team of mechanical engineers. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we are interested in tackling Flame in Freefall by combining combustion physics, engineering analysis, NASA experimental data, and AI/ML to develop a practical fire-safety prototype for future space missions.
summary:
Fire has struck crews before, from Apollo 1 to Mir, and in April 2026 a smoke detector went off on Artemis II. Future Moon and Mars bases will lower cabin pressure to shorten spacewalk preparation, which means raising oxygen to about 30–34%, an “atmosphere of increased burning” under fire codes. Yet NASA has never burned a real cabin material in microgravity in that air.

We built Flame in Freefall, a live dashboard that combines NASA’s 24 microgravity combustion investigations (2,947 test runs) into one map. Pick a habitat and what could burn, and it gives the fire risk, predicts whether a flame would go out by itself (79–89% accurate on unseen tests), and shows how much NASA data stands behind each answer.

It also reveals the gap: only 44 tests sit near Moon-base air, and none use real cabin materials. That tells NASA exactly what to test next, before crews move in.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Flame in Freefall is a live web dashboard that turns NASA's 24 microgravity combustion investigations (2,947 test runs from the ISS) into fire-safety answers for future habitats.

- Fire risk check: pick a place (ISS, cargo ship, spacewalk-prep cabin, Moon base, lunar rover, Mars base, spacesuit) and a material, and get a risk level matched to the closest real NASA test.

- Will it go out? Predicts whether a fuel drop or gas flame goes out by itself, showing the most similar real ISS fires and warning when a question goes past what NASA tested. Accuracy on unseen tests: 79% for fuel drops (vs 68% guessing) and 89% for gas flames (vs 77%).

- Turn off the fans? In NASA's BASS experiment only 10 of 106 solid fires went out when the airflow stopped.

- Oxygen map and trade-off chart: every test placed by oxygen and pressure, against the NFPA 99B fire-code line.

- Data gaps, ranking of all 24 investigations, lessons from past fires, and an Ask-the-data chat grounded in NASA documents.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Moon and Mars bases will lower pressure to shorten spacewalk prep, raising oxygen to 30-34%. Our map shows only 44 NASA tests near Moon-base air and zero on real cabin materials. The tool helps habitat designers check fire risk in seconds and points NASA to the tests that matter most: real cabin materials at 30-34% oxygen and 8-10 psi, and fires at Moon and Mars gravity.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, scikit-learn) to fetch, clean and combine the NASA PSI tables, with every value marked measured or assumed. k-nearest-neighbour predictors (K=15 fuel drops, K=9 gas flames) checked with leave-one-out cross-validation; gradient-boosting models for burn rate, burn time and smoke growth checked with 5-fold cross-validation (R² 0.65, 0.59, 0.89). React, TypeScript and ECharts, hosted on Vercel. The cleaned dataset is public on GitHub: https://github.com/yousifashraf89/FLAME-IN-FREE-FALL

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

Nobody had put NASA's combustion investigations side by side; combining them revealed the Moon-air gap. Every answer shows the real NASA tests behind it, so engineers can check it. We tested whether the gap depends on our definition of "near Moon air": widening the window to 116 tests still gives zero solid materials. Next step: most of NASA's 13.5 TB archive is flame video, and computer vision could turn it into thousands of new data points.
